passages.title: The Slowest Runner
text: Everybody in Primary Three knew that Kai was the slowest runner in the class.

It was not something anyone was unkind about. It was simply a fact, like knowing that Nadia was the tallest or that Mr Rahim's classroom was the one with the broken clock. When we picked teams, Kai was picked last, and Kai did not seem to mind.
On Sports Day, our class had to run a relay. Four runners, one baton, once around the field.
Mr Rahim chose Kai to run the last leg.
The whole class went very quiet.
"Sir," said Nadia carefully, "shouldn't the fastest person go last?"
"Usually," said Mr Rahim. "Not today."
He did not explain, and there was no time to argue.

On the day, our first three runners were wonderful. By the time the baton reached Kai, we were nearly ten metres ahead. Kai ran as fast as he could, which was not very fast, and two other runners passed him in the last twenty metres.
We came third.
Nobody said anything unkind, but nobody said anything at all either, which was somehow worse. Kai sat on the grass with his back to us.
Then Mr Rahim knelt down beside him and said something none of us could hear, and Kai laughed.
Afterwards, on the bus, Mr Rahim told us. Kai had asked him, three weeks earlier, whether he could please run in something, just once, and Mr Rahim had said yes.
"He knew he would come third," Mr Rahim said. "He asked anyway. I think that is the bravest thing that happened on that field today."
We won the relay the following year. Kai ran the last leg again, and we still won, because by then he had been practising for a year.

questions.q: What did everybody know about Kai? (1m)
questions.a: That he was the slowest runner in the Primary Three class.

questions.q: Why was the class surprised that Kai ran the last leg? (2m)
questions.a: Because the last leg is usually given to the fastest runner in the team, and Kai was the slowest, so they expected the team to lose their lead.
questions.tip: Nadia's question tells you the reason.

questions.q: What happened during the race? (2m)
questions.a: The first three runners built a lead of nearly ten metres, but two runners overtook Kai in the last twenty metres, so the class finished third.
questions.tip: Two marks: the lead, then what happened to it.

questions.q: Why does the writer say the silence was "somehow worse"? (2m)
questions.a: Because saying nothing at all made Kai feel blamed without anyone having to say so, which was harder to bear than an unkind remark he could have answered.
questions.tip: 'Why do you think' style — you have to work it out.

questions.q: Why had Mr Rahim chosen Kai? (2m)
questions.a: Because Kai had asked him three weeks earlier whether he could take part in something just once, and Mr Rahim had agreed.

questions.q: What did Mr Rahim mean by calling it "the bravest thing that happened on that field"? (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, Kai knew before he started that he would probably lose the lead. In addition, he asked to run anyway, in front of the whole school. Finally, Mr Rahim is saying that choosing to try when you expect to fail takes more courage than winning does.

questions.q: What does the last paragraph tell us about Kai? (2m)
questions.a: That he kept practising for a whole year after the race, which shows he was determined and did not let the defeat stop him.
questions.tip: The word 'because' at the end is doing the work.

questions.q: Do you think Mr Rahim made the right decision? Give a reason. (2m)
questions.a: Yes, because although the class lost the race, Kai gained the confidence to keep practising, and the class learnt something about courage that mattered more than one relay. (An answer saying no is accepted if it is well reasoned.)
questions.tip: Either answer can score, as long as you give a reason from the passage.

passages.title: Why Leaves Change Colour
text: In many countries, the leaves on certain trees turn yellow, orange or red before they fall. In Singapore, this rarely happens. The reason has less to do with the trees themselves than with the weather.

Leaves are green because they contain a substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll allows a plant to use sunlight to make its own food. Because there is so much of it in a healthy leaf, its strong green colour hides all the other colours that are also present.

Those other colours have been there the whole time. Yellow and orange come from substances called carotenoids, the same ones that make carrots orange. They simply cannot be seen while the chlorophyll is there.

In countries with cold winters, the days grow shorter in autumn and the temperature drops. The tree senses this and begins to shut down its leaves, because keeping them alive through winter would cost more energy than it gains. It stops making new chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll already in the leaf slowly breaks down.
As the green fades, the yellows and oranges that were hidden underneath become visible. Some trees also produce a red substance at this time, which is why maple leaves turn such a bright red.
Eventually the tree seals off the leaf completely, and it falls.

Singapore has no cold season and very little change in day length, so most of our trees keep their leaves all year and stay green. A few, such as the sea almond, do drop their leaves and turn a reddish colour first — but they do it whenever they are ready, not all at the same time.
So the colours of autumn are not new colours arriving. They are old colours being uncovered.

questions.q: What makes leaves green? (1m)
What does chlorophyll do for a plant? (1m)
questions.a: It lets the plant use sunlight to make its own food.

questions.q: Why can we not normally see the yellow and orange in a leaf? (2m)
questions.a: Because a healthy leaf contains so much chlorophyll that its strong green colour covers up the other colours, even though they are present all along.
questions.tip: Two marks: the amount of chlorophyll, and the effect.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why a tree shuts down its leaves in autumn. (2m)
questions.a: Keeping the leaves alive during the cold months would use up more energy than the tree would get back from them, so it is not worth doing.
questions.tip: 'Cost more energy than it gains' must be reworded.

questions.q: What two signals tell the tree that autumn has arrived? (2m)
questions.a: The days become shorter and the temperature falls.

questions.q: Why do maple leaves turn bright red rather than yellow? (1m)
questions.a: Because some trees also make a red substance at that time of year.

questions.q: Why do most trees in Singapore stay green? (2m)
questions.a: Because Singapore has no cold season and the length of the day barely changes, so the trees never receive the signals that cause leaves to shut down.
questions.tip: Link it back to the two signals in paragraph 4.

questions.q: Explain the last sentence: "They are old colours being uncovered." (3m)
questions.a: Firstly, it means the yellows and oranges were inside the leaf all along. In addition, nothing new is made when a leaf changes colour — the green is simply removed. Finally, the sentence sums up the whole passage in a single idea, which is that autumn reveals rather than creates.
questions.tip: Three marks. The third point is about why the writer ends there.
